content: {"rule":"K-C","applies":"yes","applies_why":"The judge text is deciding whether Matthew 1:16 is underdetermined by asking whether the passive verb or the opposing texts state a contrary in their own words, which is exactly the stating-verse inquiry K-C governs when a pressing side's own chain is read together.","verdict":"BREACH","quote":"D1 vs C3 (Matthew 1:16): UNDERDETERMINED -- the passive egennēthē states no verdict on the begetter in either direction, and the defender answered Luke 1:27, Luke 2:4 and Numbers 1:2 in [CR2] section A.3 and [CR3]; the verb change is real [L1]/[L2] but neither text's own words state the other reading's contrary.","rule_words":"When the witnesses pressed against a link are the pressing side's own chain read together, the collision weighs chain against chain by footing, never verse by verse; that no one of them states the contrary in its own words is the stating-verse test DG-61 retires, at a judge's seat as at a debater's, for either side.","room":"Phrase: “that no one of them states the contrary in its own words.” I weighed (1) a bar on using the absence of an explicit contrary as decisive when chains are weighed by footing versus (2) a permissible verse-by-verse stating-verse test.","why":"The judge makes the absence of a stated contrary in the passive verb and the opposed texts decisive for UNDERDETERMINED, instead of weighing the defender’s chain against the challenger’s chain by footing as K-C requires."}
